subject: math
title: Ratios: Part to Part, Part to Whole, Equivalent Ratios and Ratio Tables
seo_title: Grade 6 Ratios Worksheets (BC Curriculum) – Free Math with Answer Key
meta_desc: Free Grade 6 ratio worksheets for the BC math curriculum: write part-to-part and part-to-whole ratios, find equivalent ratios, use ratio tables, compare ratios and solve recipe and team problems. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: A ratio compares two amounts in order. Multiply or divide both terms by the same number to get an equivalent ratio.
key_sub: Red to blue 3:5 is part to part; red to all 3:8 is part to whole (3/8). Never add the same number to both terms.
body_html:
What a ratio is

A ratio compares two amounts. 3:5 is read “3 to 5”. Keep the order of the words: red to blue means the red number comes first.

A part-to-part ratio compares two parts. A part-to-whole ratio compares one part with everything. Part to whole can also be written as a fraction.

Equivalent ratios

Multiply or divide both terms by the same number. The ratio stays the same. Never add the same number to both terms.

Example

Find the missing term: 2:3 = ?:12

3 × 4 = 12, so multiply 2 by 4 too.

Answer: 8

Simplest form

Write 12:16 in simplest form.

Divide both terms by 4: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 and 16 ÷ 4 = 4.

Answer: 3:4

Ratio tables

Each column of a ratio table is the first column times a number.

Comparing ratios

Make one term the same, then compare the other term.

Example

Mix A is juice to water 2:3. Mix B is 4:5. Which tastes more of juice?

2:3 = 4:6. Both now have 4 cups of juice. Mix B has less water (5 < 6).

Answer: Mix B

Part of a total

A team has boys and girls in the ratio 3:5. There are 24 players. How many are boys?

Each group has 3 + 5 = 8 players. 24 ÷ 8 = 3 groups. Boys: 3 × 3 = 9.

Answer: 9 boys

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
3 red and 5 blue: red to blue is 5:3Keep the order of the words: red to blue is 3:5
Red to blue is 3:5, so 35 are red3:5 is part to part. The whole is 3 + 5 = 8, so 38 are red
2:3 = 5:6 (add 3 to both)Multiply both terms: 2:3 = 6:9
1:5 is stronger than 1:2 because 5 is biggerMake one term the same, then compare. 1:2 has less water

faq.q: What do Grade 6 students learn about ratios in BC?
faq.a: The BC Grade 6 math curriculum introduces ratios. Students write part-to-part and part-to-whole ratios, find equivalent ratios, use ratio tables and compare ratios in real situations like recipes and teams.

faq.q: What is the difference between a part-to-part and a part-to-whole ratio?
faq.a: Part to part compares two groups, like 3 red to 5 blue (3:5). Part to whole compares one group with everything, like 3 red out of 8 counters (3:8), which is the fraction 3/8.

faq.q: How do you find equivalent ratios?
faq.a: Multiply or divide both terms by the same number: 2:3 = 4:6 = 6:9. Adding the same number to both terms (2:3 to 5:6) does not give an equivalent ratio.

faq.q: How do you compare two ratios?
faq.a: Make one term the same in both ratios, then compare the other term. For juice to water, 2:3 = 4:6, so 4:5 has less water and tastes stronger.

sets.title: Writing ratios from pictures: part to part and part to whole

items.q: What is the ratio of red counters to blue counters?
items.e: 3 red and 4 blue. Red is named first, so the ratio is 3:4. 4:3 is blue to red, and 3:7 is red to all the counters.

items.q: What is the ratio of blue counters to red counters?
items.e: Blue is named first: 2 blue, then 5 red, so 2:5. 5:2 has the terms in the wrong order, and 2:7 compares blue to all 7 counters.

items.q: What is the ratio of red counters to all the counters?
items.e: This is part to whole. There are 4 + 3 = 7 counters, and 4 are red: 4:7. 4:3 is red to blue (part to part), and 3:7 is blue to all.

items.q: What is the ratio of blue counters to all the counters?
items.e: There are 2 + 6 = 8 counters, and 6 are blue: 6:8. 6:2 is blue to yellow (part to part), and 8:6 has the terms in the wrong order.

items.q: What is the ratio of blue counters to green counters?
items.e: Blue is named first: 5 blue to 3 green, so 5:3. 3:5 is green to blue, and 5:8 is blue to all the counters.

items.q: What is the ratio of shaded squares to unshaded squares?
items.e: 3 squares are shaded and 8 − 3 = 5 are not: 3:5. 3:8 is shaded to the whole grid (part to whole).

items.q: What is the ratio of shaded squares to all the squares?
items.e: The grid has 3 × 3 = 9 squares, and 4 are shaded: 4:9. 4:5 is shaded to unshaded, and 5:9 is unshaded to all.

items.q: What is the ratio of unshaded squares to shaded squares?
items.e: 10 − 6 = 4 squares are unshaded and 6 are shaded. Unshaded comes first: 4:6. 6:4 is shaded to unshaded, and 4:10 is unshaded to all.

items.q: What is the ratio of shaded squares to unshaded squares?
items.e: 5 shaded and 7 − 5 = 2 unshaded: 5:2. 2:5 has the terms in the wrong order, and 5:7 is shaded to all.

items.q: What is the ratio of red to blue to yellow counters?
items.e: Keep the order of the words: 2 red, 3 blue, 4 yellow, so 2:3:4. 4:3:2 is yellow to blue to red, and 9 is the total, not the yellow.

items.q: What is the ratio of blue counters to all the counters?
items.e: There are 3 + 1 + 4 = 8 counters, and 1 is blue: 1:8. 1:7 is blue to the other counters (part to part), and 1:4 is blue to yellow.

items.q: Which statement about the counters is not true?
items.e: There are 4 red and 2 blue. Blue to red puts blue first, so it is 2:4, not 4:2. The false statement is Blue to red is 4:2. The other three are true.

items.q: Finish the sentence: “For every 1 blue counter, there are ___ red counters.”
items.e: 6 red and 2 blue. Split them into 2 equal groups: each group has 1 blue and 6 ÷ 2 = 3 red. 6 is all the red, 4 is the difference 6 − 2, and 8 is all the counters.

items.q: Finish the sentence: “For every 1 red counter, there are ___ blue counters.”
items.e: 8 blue shared between 2 red is 8 ÷ 2 = 4 blue for each red. 8 is all the blue, 6 is the difference 8 − 2, and 10 is all the counters.

items.q: What fraction of the grid is shaded?
items.e: A fraction is part to whole. 4 of the 2 × 6 = 12 squares are shaded: 412. 48 compares shaded to unshaded (part to part), and 812 is the unshaded part.

items.q: Which sentence describes the counters?
c: For every 1 red, there are 2 blue
For every 1 red, there are 3 blue
For every 2 red, there is 1 blue
For every 1 red, there are 6 blue
items.e: 3 red and 6 blue. Make 3 groups: each has 1 red and 6 ÷ 3 = 2 blue, so for every 1 red, there are 2 blue. “2 red for 1 blue” has the order backwards.

items.q: Kai adds 1 more blue counter. What is the new ratio of red to blue counters?
items.e: Blue goes from 3 to 3 + 1 = 4. Red stays 5. The new ratio is 5:4. 6:4 adds 1 to the red too, and 5:9 is red to all the counters.

items.q: What is the ratio of unshaded squares to all the squares?
items.e: The grid has 3 × 4 = 12 squares. 12 − 9 = 3 are unshaded: 3:12. 3:9 is unshaded to shaded, and 9:12 is shaded to all.

items.q: Which two colours are in the ratio 2:1?
items.e: Red to blue is 4:2. For every 2 red there is 1 blue, so 4:2 is the same as 2:1: red to blue. Blue to red is 2:4, which is 1:2, the wrong order.

items.q: Nadia says the ratio of red counters to blue counters is 5:3. What mistake did she make?
c: She wrote the terms in the wrong order
She counted the red counters wrong
She compared red with all the counters
items.e: There are 3 red and 5 blue. Red is named first, so the ratio is 3:5. Nadia wrote 5:3, which is blue to red: she wrote the terms in the wrong order.

items.q: Which ratio is equivalent to 1:3?
items.e: Multiply both terms by 2: 1 × 2 = 2 and 3 × 2 = 6, so 1:3 = 2:6. 2:4 adds 1 to both terms, and 2:3 multiplies only the first term.

items.q: Which ratio is equivalent to 2:5?
items.e: 2 × 2 = 4 and 5 × 2 = 10, so 2:5 = 4:10. 4:7 adds 2 to both terms, and 4:5 doubles only the 2.

items.q: Which ratio is equivalent to 3:4?
items.e: 3 × 3 = 9 and 4 × 3 = 12, so 3:4 = 9:12. 6:7 adds 3 to both terms, and 9:4 multiplies only the 3.

items.q: Multiply both terms of 4:7 by 3. What equivalent ratio do you get?
items.e: 4 × 3 = 12 and 7 × 3 = 21: 12:21. 12:7 forgets the second term, 7:10 adds 3 instead of multiplying, and 21:12 has the terms in the wrong order.

items.q: Find the missing term: 2:3 = ?:12
items.e: 3 × 4 = 12, so multiply the first term by 4 too: 2 × 4 = 8. 11 adds 9, like 3 + 9 = 12, but equivalent ratios never come from adding. 4 is only the number you multiply by.

items.q: Find the missing term: 5:2 = 15:?
items.e: 5 × 3 = 15, so multiply 2 by 3 too: 6. 12 adds 10 like 5 + 10 = 15, 3 is the number you multiply by, and 30 multiplies 15 by 2.

items.q: Find the missing term: 4:9 = 20:?
items.e: 4 × 5 = 20, so 9 × 5 = 45. 25 adds 16 to both terms, 5 is the number you multiply by, and 36 multiplies 9 by 4.

items.q: Find the missing term: 6:8 = 3:?
items.e: 6 ÷ 2 = 3, so divide 8 by 2 too: 4. 5 subtracts 3 from both terms, 2 is the number you divide by, and 16 multiplies instead of dividing.

items.q: Write 6:9 in simplest form.
items.e: 3 is the greatest number that divides both 6 and 9. 6 ÷ 3 = 2 and 9 ÷ 3 = 3: 2:3. 3:6 subtracts 3 from both terms, and 2:9 divides only the first term.

items.q: Write 12:16 in simplest form.
items.e: Divide both terms by 4: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 and 16 ÷ 4 = 4, so 3:4. 6:10 subtracts 6 from both terms, and 3:16 divides only the 12.

items.q: Write 16:12 in simplest form.
items.e: Divide both terms by 4: 16 ÷ 4 = 4 and 12 ÷ 4 = 3, so 4:3. 3:4 has the terms in the wrong order, and 8:4 subtracts 8 from both terms.

items.q: Which ratio is not equivalent to 2:3?
items.e: 4:6, 6:9 and 10:15 are 2:3 times 2, 3 and 5. 5:6 adds 3 to both terms, so it is not equivalent.

items.q: Which ratio is not equivalent to 4:5?
items.e: 8:10, 12:15 and 40:50 are 4:5 times 2, 3 and 10. 6:7 adds 2 to both terms, so it is not equivalent.

items.q: Liam says 3:4 = 5:6 because he added 2 to both terms. Is he right?
c: Yes. Add the same number to both terms
Yes. Both terms went up by 2
items.e: Equivalent ratios come from multiplying (or dividing) both terms by the same number. 3:4 × 2 = 6:8. Adding 2 gives 5:6, which is a different ratio.

items.q: Are 2:5 and 6:15 equivalent ratios?
c: No. 6 − 2 is not the same as 15 − 5
items.e: 2 × 3 = 6 and 5 × 3 = 15, so yes, they are equivalent. Checking by subtracting does not work for ratios.

items.q: Find the missing term: ?:7 = 18:21
items.e: 7 × 3 = 21, so the missing term times 3 is 18. 18 ÷ 3 = 6. 4 subtracts 14 from both terms, 3 is the number you multiply by, and 54 multiplies 18 by 3.

items.q: Find the missing term: 7:3 = 28:?
items.e: 7 × 4 = 28, so 3 × 4 = 12. 24 adds 21 like 7 + 21 = 28, and 84 multiplies 28 by 3.

items.q: Which pair shows two equivalent ratios?
items.e: 3 × 3 = 9 and 5 × 3 = 15, so 3:5 and 9:15 are equivalent. 5:7 and 6:8 add the same number to both terms, and 5:3 has the terms in the other order.

items.q: Which ratio is equivalent to 12:18 and in simplest form?
items.e: Divide both terms by 6, the greatest common factor: 12:18 = 2:3. 6:9 and 4:6 are equivalent too, but they can still be simplified. 3:2 is the wrong order.

items.q: Which list shows ratios equivalent to 3:5?
items.e: Multiply both terms by 2, 3 and 4: 6:10, 9:15, 12:20. 4:6, 5:7, 6:8 adds 1 each time, 6:5 multiplies only the first term, and 5:3, 10:6, 15:9 has the terms in the wrong order.

sets.title: Ratio tables and double number lines

items.q: The table shows juice mixed with water. What number is missing?
items.e: The top row is 1 × 1, 1 × 2, 1 × 3. Do the same to the bottom row: 3 × 3 = 9. 7 adds 1 like the top row, 12 doubles 6, and 18 multiplies 6 by 3.

items.q: Each canoe holds the same number of people. What number is missing?
items.e: Each canoe holds 2 people, so 4 canoes hold 4 × 2 = 8. 7 adds 1 like the top row, 12 doubles 6, and 24 multiplies 6 by 4.

items.q: The table shows bags of apples. What number is missing?
items.e: 6 = 2 × 3, so multiply 5 by 3 too: 15. 12 adds 2 like the top row, 20 doubles 10, and 30 multiplies 5 by 6.

items.q: A pancake recipe uses eggs and milk in the same ratio. What number is missing?
items.e: There are 2 eggs for every 1 cup of milk. 5 cups need 5 × 2 = 10 eggs. 7 adds 3 like 2 + 3 = 5, 5 copies the milk, and 6 is only the next step after 4.

items.q: Kai reads at a steady pace. What number is missing?
items.e: The minutes are halved: 4 ÷ 2 = 2. Halve the pages too: 12 ÷ 2 = 6. 10 subtracts 2 like the minutes row, 8 subtracts 4, and 3 divides 12 by 4.

items.q: Sofia hikes at a steady pace. What number is missing?
items.e: She hikes 4 km in 1 hour. In 5 hours: 5 × 4 = 20 km. 14 adds 2 like the hours row, 16 adds one more 4, and 60 multiplies 12 by 5.

items.q: What ratio of red beads to white beads does the table show?
items.e: Every column is 3 red to 2 white, times a number: 3:2. 2:3 has the terms in the wrong order, 3:5 is red to all the beads, and 3:6 reads along the top row instead of down a column.

items.q: A ratio table shows the ratio 2:7. Which column could be in the table?
items.e: Multiply both terms by 4: 2 × 4 = 8 and 7 × 4 = 28, so 8 and 28. “8 and 13” and “4 and 9” add the same number to both terms, and “7 and 2” is the wrong order.

items.q: Which is a ratio table?
items.e: In a ratio table, every column is the first column times a number. 1:6, 2:12 and 3:18 are all 1:6 times 1, 2 and 3, so 1, 2, 3 and 6, 12, 18. The others add to a row, or (in the last one) 4:18 is not 1:6.

items.q: A rice recipe makes servings in the same ratio. What number is missing?
items.e: 6 = 2 × 3, so multiply 6 by 3 too: 6 × 3 = 18 servings. 14 adds 2 like the top row, 36 multiplies 6 by 6, and 16 adds 4 to 12.

items.q: Owen runs laps at a steady pace. How many minutes does 6 laps take?
items.e: 2 laps take 5 minutes. 6 laps is 3 × 2 laps, so 3 × 5 = 15 minutes. 12 adds 2 like the laps row, 20 doubles 10, and 30 multiplies 5 by 6.

items.q: Each ticket for the school play costs the same. What is the cost of 2 tickets?
items.e: 1 ticket costs $4, so 2 tickets cost 2 × $4 = $8. $5 adds 1 like the ticket row, $6 is half of $12, and $24 doubles the $12 instead of the $4.

items.q: On a field trip there are 4 kids for every adult. How many kids go with 10 adults?
items.e: Each adult has 4 kids, so 10 adults go with 10 × 4 = 40 kids. 16 just counts on by 4, 19 adds 7 like 3 + 7 = 10, and 14 adds 10 to 4.

items.q: A muffin recipe uses eggs in the same ratio. How many muffins can you make with 1 egg?
items.e: 2 eggs make 6 muffins, so halve both: 1 egg makes 6 ÷ 2 = 3 muffins. 4 subtracts 2 like 6 − 2, 5 subtracts 1 like the egg row, and 1 copies the eggs.

items.q: A cookie recipe uses sugar in the same ratio. How many cups of sugar make 120 cookies?
items.e: 1 cup makes 24 cookies. 120 ÷ 24 = 5 cups. 3 only counts on by 1, 72 is the number of cookies for 3 cups, and 6 divides 120 by 20.

items.q: Green and blue paint are mixed in the same ratio. What number is missing?
items.e: 6 = 3 × 2, so multiply 5 by 2 too: 10. Check: 9:15 is 3:5 × 3. 8 adds 3 like the top row, 12 doubles 6, and 30 multiplies 6 by 5.

items.q: A canoe moves at a steady speed. How far does it go in 4 hours?
items.e: The canoe goes 3 km each hour. 4 hours: 4 × 3 = 12 km. 9 counts on by 3, but the hours jumped from 2 to 4. 8 adds 2, and 24 multiplies 6 by 4.

items.q: Every packet holds the same number of seeds. What number is missing?
items.e: 4 packets hold 36 seeds, so 1 packet holds 36 ÷ 4 = 9. 54 ÷ 9 = 6 packets. 8 doubles 4, 22 adds 18 like 36 + 18 = 54, and 9 is the seeds in 1 packet.

items.q: Mei wants every column to show the same ratio. Which column does not belong?
items.e: The ratio is 2:5, so the scoops are 5 × (cups ÷ 2). 6 cups need 3 × 5 = 15 scoops, not 13. 6 and 13 does not belong. The others are 2:5 times 1, 2 and 4.

items.q: A bracelet pattern uses beads in the ratio shown. How many yellow beads go with 30 red beads?
items.e: 30 = 3 × 10, so yellow = 4 × 10 = 40. 34 adds 4 to 30, 31 adds 1 (the difference between 3 and 4), and 120 multiplies 30 by 4.

items.q: Mix A has juice and water in the ratio 1:2. Mix B has juice and water in the ratio 1:3. Which mix tastes more of juice?
items.e: Both use 1 cup of juice. Mix A adds only 2 cups of water, Mix B adds 3. Less water for the same juice means Mix A is stronger. Bigger numbers do not mean more juice.

items.q: Paint A uses red and white in the ratio 2:5. Paint B uses red and white in the ratio 2:3. Which paint is a darker red?
items.e: Both use 2 parts red. Paint B adds only 3 parts white, so it is Paint B. Paint A has more white, so it is a lighter pink.

items.q: Lemonade A has lemon juice and water in the ratio 3:4. Lemonade B has the ratio 6:8. Which tastes more of lemon?
items.e: 6:8 = 3:4 × 2. The ratios are equivalent, so they are the same. Lemonade B is just a bigger batch.

items.q: Mix A has juice and water in the ratio 2:3. Mix B has juice and water in the ratio 4:5. Which mix tastes more of juice?
items.e: Make the juice the same: 2:3 = 4:6. Now compare 4:6 with 4:5. Mix B has less water for 4 cups of juice, so Mix B. Both have 1 more cup of water than juice, but that does not make them equal.

items.q: The Kelowna team’s ratio of wins to losses is 4:2. The Kamloops team’s ratio of wins to losses is 6:4. Which team has the better record?
items.e: Make the wins the same: 4:2 = 2:1 = 6:3. Compare 6:3 with 6:4. Kelowna loses fewer games for the same 6 wins, so Kelowna. Kamloops has more wins, but also more losses.

items.q: In Class A the ratio of boys to girls is 3:4. In Class B it is 5:4. In which class are there more boys than girls?
items.e: In 5:4, the first term (boys) is bigger, so Class B has more boys than girls. In Class A, 3:4 means fewer boys than girls.

items.q: Mix A uses 2 scoops of powder for 6 cups of water. Mix B uses 3 scoops for 9 cups. Which mix is stronger?
items.e: 2:6 = 1:3 and 3:9 = 1:3. Both are 1 scoop for every 3 cups, so they are the same.

items.q: Hot chocolate A uses cocoa and milk in the ratio 3:4. Hot chocolate B uses the ratio 5:8. Which tastes more of chocolate?
items.e: Make the milk the same: 3:4 = 6:8. Compare 6:8 with 5:8. A has more cocoa in 8 cups of milk, so Hot chocolate A.

items.q: At Shelter A the ratio of dogs to cats is 5:10. At Shelter B it is 4:6. Which shelter has more dogs for each cat?
items.e: 5:10 = 1:2, so Shelter A has 1 dog for every 2 cats (3:6). Shelter B has 4:6. 4 > 3, so Shelter B. Shelter A has bigger numbers, but not more dogs per cat.

items.q: Which juice mix (concentrate to water) is the strongest?
items.e: All four use 1 part concentrate. The one with the least water is strongest: 1:2. 1:5 has the most water, so it is the weakest, even though 5 is the biggest number.

items.q: Which juice mix (concentrate to water) is the weakest?
items.e: All four use 2 parts concentrate. The one with the most water is weakest: 2:7.

items.q: Trail Mix A has raisins and nuts in the ratio 2:3. Trail Mix B has the ratio 3:2. Which mix has more raisins than nuts?
items.e: In 3:2 the raisins (first term) are more than the nuts, so Trail Mix B. The order of the terms matters: 2:3 and 3:2 are different ratios.

items.q: Ji-woo says 3:5 and 5:7 are equivalent because both have a difference of 2. Is she right?
c: Yes. Both have a difference of 2
items.e: Make the second terms the same: 3:5 × 7 = 21:35 and 5:7 × 5 = 25:35. 21 is not 25, so no. The difference does not tell you if ratios are equivalent. (5:7 is not 6:8.)

items.q: Kai mixes blue and yellow paint in the ratio 1:3. Zara mixes them in the ratio 2:5. Whose green paint is bluer?
items.e: Make the blue the same: 1:3 = 2:6. Compare 2:6 with 2:5. Zara uses less yellow for 2 parts blue, so Zara’s paint is bluer.

items.q: Hana scored 6 goals in 8 hockey games. Owen scored 9 goals in 12 games. Who has the better ratio of goals to games?
items.e: 6:8 = 3:4 and 9:12 = 3:4. Both scored 3 goals for every 4 games, so they are the same. Owen has more goals, but he also played more games.

items.q: Which ratio of red counters to blue counters has the most red for each blue?
items.e: Find the red for 1 blue: 3:1 is 3, 5:2 is 2.5, 8:4 is 2, and 7:3 is a little more than 2. The most is 3:1. 8:4 has the biggest numbers but only 2 red for each blue.

items.q: In Tray A, 12 of 16 seeds sprouted. In Tray B, 14 of 20 seeds sprouted. Which tray has the greater ratio of sprouted seeds to seeds planted?
items.e: 12:16 = 3:4 = 15:20. Compare 15:20 with 14:20. Tray A is greater. Tray B has more sprouted seeds, but more seeds were planted.

items.q: In Class A, 8 of 24 students bike to school. In Class B, 9 of 30 students bike. Which class has the greater ratio of bikers to all students?
items.e: 8:24 = 1:3 = 10:30. Compare 10:30 with 9:30. Class A is greater, even though Class B has more bikers.

items.q: A drink uses 2 scoops of powder for 5 cups of water. Which mix tastes the same?
items.e: 2:5 × 2 = 4:10, so 4 scoops for 10 cups tastes the same. 4 scoops for 7 cups and 5 scoops for 8 cups add the same number to both terms, and 3:6 = 1:2 is stronger.

items.q: Mix A has juice and water in the ratio 3:7. Mix B has juice and water in the ratio 4:9. Which mix tastes more of juice?
items.e: Make the water the same: 3:7 × 9 = 27:63 and 4:9 × 7 = 28:63. 28 > 27, so Mix B has a little more juice.

items.q: A pancake recipe uses 3 cups of flour for every 2 eggs. Mei uses 9 cups of flour. How many eggs does she need?
items.e: 3 × 3 = 9, so multiply the eggs by 3 too: 2 × 3 = 6 eggs. 8 adds 6 like 3 + 6 = 9, 3 is the number you multiply by, and 18 multiplies 9 by 2.

items.q: On a soccer team, the ratio of boys to girls is 2:3. There are 8 boys. How many girls are there?
items.e: 2 × 4 = 8, so the girls are 3 × 4 = 12. 9 adds 6 like 2 + 6 = 8, 20 is the whole team, and 4 is the number you multiply by.

items.q: A hockey team has 12 forwards and 6 defence players. What is the ratio of forwards to defence players in simplest form?
items.e: 12:6. Divide both terms by 6: 2:1. 1:2 is defence to forwards, 2:3 is 12:18, forwards to the whole team, and 1:3 is defence to the whole team.

items.q: Trail mix for a hike on Vancouver Island uses 3 cups of nuts for every 2 cups of raisins. How many cups of raisins go with 12 cups of nuts?
items.e: 3 × 4 = 12, so 2 × 4 = 8 cups. 11 adds 9 like 3 + 9 = 12, and 18 uses the ratio the wrong way round (12 ÷ 2 × 3).

items.q: A smoothie recipe uses 2 bananas for 4 people. How many bananas are needed for 10 people?
items.e: 2 bananas for 4 people is 1 banana for every 2 people. 10 ÷ 2 = 5 bananas. 8 adds 6 because there are 6 more people, 20 multiplies 2 by 10, and 10 gives 1 banana each.

items.q: In a volleyball club, the ratio of Grade 6 players to Grade 7 players is 3:5. There are 24 players in all. How many are in Grade 6?
items.e: Each group has 3 + 5 = 8 players. 24 ÷ 8 = 3 groups. Grade 6: 3 × 3 = 9. 15 is the Grade 7 players, 8 divides 24 by 3, and 12 is just half the club.

items.q: A muffin recipe uses 2 cups of oats to make 12 muffins. How many muffins can you make with 5 cups of oats?
items.e: 1 cup makes 12 ÷ 2 = 6 muffins. 5 cups make 5 × 6 = 30. 15 adds 3 like 2 + 3 = 5, 60 multiplies 12 by 5, and 24 is for 4 cups.

items.q: At the school’s Terry Fox Run, the ratio of students who walked to students who ran was 5:3. 15 students ran. How many walked?
items.e: 3 × 5 = 15, so the walkers are 5 × 5 = 25. 17 adds 12 like 3 + 12 = 15, 9 uses the ratio the wrong way round, and 40 is everyone.

items.q: A basketball team’s ratio of wins to losses is 3:2. They played 20 games with no ties. How many games did they win?
items.e: Each group has 3 + 2 = 5 games. 20 ÷ 5 = 4 groups. Wins: 3 × 4 = 12. 8 is the losses, 10 is just half the games, and 4 is the number of groups.

items.q: Olivia makes 16 tablespoons of salad dressing with oil and vinegar in the ratio 3:1. How much oil does she use?
items.e: Each batch has 3 + 1 = 4 parts. 16 ÷ 4 = 4 tablespoons per part. Oil is 3 parts: 12 tablespoons. 4 is the vinegar, 48 multiplies 16 by 3, and 15 takes away just 1.

items.q: A hockey coach brings 3 oranges for every 4 players. There are 16 players. How many oranges does the coach bring?
items.e: 4 × 4 = 16, so 3 × 4 = 12 oranges. 15 adds 12 like 4 + 12 = 16, 4 is the number you multiply by, and 48 multiplies 16 by 3.

items.q: For an art class, Emma mixes blue and white paint in the ratio 1:4. She makes 25 mL of paint. How much white paint does she use?
items.e: Each batch has 1 + 4 = 5 parts. 25 ÷ 5 = 5 mL per part. White is 4 parts: 4 × 5 = 20 mL. 5 mL is the blue, 100 mL multiplies 25 by 4, and 6.25 mL divides by 4 instead of 5.

items.q: A chili recipe serves 8 people and uses 6 tomatoes. How many tomatoes are needed to serve 4 people?
items.e: 4 people is half of 8, so use half the tomatoes: 6 ÷ 2 = 3. 2 subtracts 4 like 8 − 4, 12 doubles instead of halving, and 4 copies the number of people.

items.q: A soccer team pays $45 for 3 new balls. At the same price, what do 7 balls cost?
items.e: 1 ball costs $45 ÷ 3 = $15. 7 balls cost 7 × $15 = $105. $49 adds $4 for 4 more balls, $315 multiplies $45 by 7, and $90 is for 6 balls.

items.q: On a BC Ferries sailing, the ratio of cars to trucks is 9:1. There are 270 cars. How many trucks are there?
items.e: 1 truck for every 9 cars: 270 ÷ 9 = 30 trucks. 262 subtracts 8, 2430 multiplies by 9, and 27 divides by 10 as if 270 were all the vehicles.

items.q: At a hockey camp in Prince George, the ratio of kids to coaches is 8:1. There are 5 coaches. How many kids are there?
items.e: Each coach has 8 kids: 5 × 8 = 40. 13 adds 8 and 5, 45 counts the coaches too, and 32 is for only 4 coaches.

items.q: In a Grade 6 class of 28 students, the ratio of students who play on a team to students who do not is 4:3. How many play on a team?
items.e: Each group has 4 + 3 = 7 students. 28 ÷ 7 = 4 groups. Team players: 4 × 4 = 16. 12 is the students who do not, 7 divides 28 by 4, and 21 is 28 ÷ 4 × 3, as if 4:3 meant 3 out of every 4.

items.q: Granola bars use 4 cups of oats for every 1 cup of honey. Ryan uses 2 cups of honey. How many cups of oats does he need?
items.e: Double the honey, so double the oats: 4 × 2 = 8 cups. 5 adds 1 like 1 + 1 = 2, 6 adds 2 to 4, and 0.5 divides 2 by 4 (the wrong way round).

items.q: The Surrey team won 7 of its 10 games. The Burnaby team won 9 of its 15 games. Which team has the greater ratio of wins to games played?
items.e: Make the games the same: 7:10 = 21:30 and 9:15 = 18:30. 21 > 18, so Surrey. Burnaby has more wins, but it played more games.

items.q: A banana bread recipe uses 2 cups of flour for every 3 bananas. Sofia has 8 cups of flour and 9 bananas. She uses all the bananas. How much flour is left over?
items.e: 9 bananas = 3 × 3 bananas, so she uses 3 × 2 = 6 cups of flour. 8 − 6 = 2 cups left over. 6 cups is the flour she uses, 1 cup is 9 − 8, and 0 cups forgets that 9 bananas need only 6 cups.
